4.2 — Patrol Polish: Bounds, Flips & Animations

The starter's patrol ships with a strange pair of guard clauses that look redundant — they are not. Today you break the patrol the way a real bug would, meet the clause that saves it, and finish the enemy so it reads alive before it ever chases you.

Predict First ~15 min

Here is the full flip block from PlatformerMove — including the part that looks useless:

float dist = Vector3.Distance(startPosition, transform.position);
if (dist > patrolDistance)
{
    direction *= -1; // Switch direction
    // Ensure we don't get stuck flipping
    if (direction == 1 && transform.position.x < startPosition.x) direction = 1;
    else if (direction == -1 && transform.position.x > startPosition.x) direction = -1;

    // Visual flip
    GetComponentInChildren<SpriteRenderer>().flipX = direction < 0;
}

Predict the scenario that needs those middle clauses. Hint: Translate runs per frame; the enemy crosses the leash boundary somewhere. Where does it stand at the moment it flips — exactly at the boundary, or a little past it? Now imagine a BIG speed: each frame moves it a lot. Flip happens at frame N; frame N+1 moves again... how could that jitter at the edge?

Then build the disease to see the cure: set speed to 15, patrolDistance to 0.1, and watch the enemy vibrate at the end of its beat. THAT is the stuck-flip the clauses prevent — flipping every frame while standing outside the leash.

Socratic

The guard clauses say: "if I am heading right but I am actually LEFT of the anchor, commit to right." Explain in your own words what state the enemy was in when the naive flip failed — and why checking reality (position) beats trusting intent (direction).

Build Lab ~20 min

Step 1 — the visual flip. The last line reads the signed state you built in 4.1 and mirrors the sprite: flipX = direction < 0. Watch the face, not the movement: walking right shows the sprite's default, walking left mirrors it. One line of code, zero art changes — a mirror is cheaper than a second sprite.

Step 2 — GetComponentInChildren, noticed. The flip line reaches the SpriteRenderer through GetComponentInChildren — the same call your PlayerController uses for its animator. Why "in children"? Because the visual sprite lives on a child object of the enemy prefab. Look at the MobileEnemy prefab in the Hierarchy: find which child carries the SpriteRenderer.

Step 3 — make it breathe. The MobileEnemy ships with animation (there is a TopDown_EnemyAnimator in the starter's Package Scripts). Play with it: if the enemy walks with its own walk cycle, the patrol stops being a sliding statue. If its animator has an idle/walk parameter, wire the same trick the player used in 1.6: code sets state, animator plays frames.

Bug Hunt: Polish gone wrong

  1. Comment out the flipX line. The enemy moonwalks — what does the player actually see, and why is this the cheapest "broken" to fix?
  2. Change flipX to direction > 0. Which direction faces correctly now, and which faces wrong?
  3. Delete BOTH guard clauses and set speed 15 / patrolDistance 0.1. Describe the vibration in frame terms: what does the enemy do each of the 60 frames per second?
  4. Flip the sprite by NEGATING the local scale instead (a classic alternative). Why can that break animations or colliders on some rigs — and why did flipX win?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Feel the guard

  1. Design a "look busy" idle: pause 0.5s at each end of the beat. What state do you add — and does the pause need its own timer field?
  2. Two enemies patrolling the SAME leash, half a beat apart. When the player watches them cross, what does the crossing look like — and can you make them collide?
  3. Commit + push: "4.2a: patrol polish + flip read".

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Demonstrate the stuck-flip bug and explain the guard clauses that prevent it
  • Explain flipX as a mirror driven by signed state
  • Say what GetComponentInChildren does and why the enemy needs it
  • Wire enemy animation the same way the player's works
